transcript_segments.text: What changes when you tell an AI note-taker, no?
On September 2nd, Tannenaut Chiefs Conference,
an interior Alaska Tribal Health Organization,
announced its introducing Sully.AI.
Its job is paperwork.
The aim is less typing and more attention for patients.
With the patient's permission,
the tool listens during the appointment and drafts a note.
That draft still has a boss.
The provider reviews it, edits it, and approves it.
Only then can it enter the medical record.
Sully isn't making medical decisions.
But does that design actually give patients more attention?
Keep that question open.
TCC gives recordings a 90-day deletion policy.
Recordings and approved notes are different things.
The technology company may also use
de-identified portions of recordings to improve the system.
TCC says recording storage follows hip-hop.
Now give the offer its strongest case.
Less typing could mean a better conversation.
And TCC tells patients about the possible reuse.
An informed yes is a reasonable choice.
But this notice reports no measured benefits.
A sensible design isn't proof that it works.
One question still matters for that informed choice.
How long can de-identified portions be kept?
Ask about those portions before deciding.
To decline, just tell your provider.
Now switch the recorder off.
TCC says you can decline or change your mind.
Your care won't be affected.
That's its promise, not an independently tested result.
Useful AI doesn't need every patient
to make the same choice.
The patient can step aside.
The care has to stay.
Would you want this note-taker at your next visit?
